title: YOUR MOUTH JUST EXPOSED YOUR HEART—AND JESUS HEARD WHAT YOU THOUGHT WAS “JUST WORDS”
paragraphs: YOUR MOUTH JUST EXPOSED YOUR HEART—AND JESUS HEARD WHAT YOU THOUGHT WAS “JUST WORDS”
What Jesus really meant by “out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks”—and why the sentence you regret saying may be revealing something God wants to heal.
There are moments when a sentence leaves your mouth...
and you immediately wish you could pull it back.
You saw their face change.
You felt the atmosphere shift.
Maybe it happened in your marriage.
Maybe you said it to your child.
Maybe you whispered it about someone after they walked away.
Maybe it came out during an argument, when anger had already climbed into your throat and wisdom arrived three seconds too late.
“I didn’t mean that.”
We say those words so quickly.
And sometimes we genuinely regret what we said.
But Jesus confronts us with an uncomfortable possibility:
What if the problem is deeper than the sentence?
What if the mouth did not create the ugliness?
What if it simply revealed where some of it had been hiding?
Jesus said:
“Out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaketh.” — Luke 6:45, KJV
The Greek is striking:
ἐκ γὰρ περισσεύματος καρδίας λαλεῖ τὸ στόμα αὐτοῦ
ek gar perisseumatos kardias lalei to stoma autou
Literally, the thought is that out of the abundance, overflow, or surplus of the heart, the mouth speaks.
The word περίσσευμα — perisseuma carries the idea of abundance, that which exceeds or overflows.

The word καρδία — kardia, translated “heart,” is not merely describing the physical organ beating inside your chest. In biblical usage, the heart can represent the inner person—the center of thought, desire, affection, intention, and will.
And then there is στόμα — stoma.
The mouth.
Jesus connects the unseen interior with the audible exterior.
The heart fills.
The mouth eventually spills.
That means your words are more than sounds.
Sometimes they are evidence.
Sometimes the sentence that embarrassed you is carrying a sample from a reservoir nobody else could see.
That is why this teaching is much more serious than, “Christians should speak nicely.”
Jesus was not giving His followers an etiquette lesson.
He was diagnosing the human heart.
And that diagnosis becomes even more uncomfortable when we hear what He said in Matthew 15:18:
τὰ δὲ ἐκπορευόμενα ἐκ τοῦ στόματος ἐκ τῆς καρδίας ἐξέρχεται
ta de ekporeuomena ek tou stomatos ek tēs kardias exerchetai
“But those things which proceed out of the mouth come forth from the heart...” — Matthew 15:18, KJV
The Greek preposition ἐκ — ek means “out of” or “from,” emphasizing origin.
Jesus is pointing upstream.
The mouth is not the ultimate source.
The heart is.
And suddenly this becomes personal.
Because most of us are experts at treating verbal symptoms while protecting the spiritual disease underneath them.
We apologize for shouting...
but never confront the pride that made us believe we deserved control.
We regret the gossip...
but never confront the insecurity that secretly enjoyed watching somebody else become smaller.
We delete the cruel comment...
but never ask why another person's success made resentment rise inside us.
We say, “I was just angry.”
Jesus asks us to look deeper.
Why did anger have those particular words available?
We say, “I was tired.”
Perhaps you were.

Fatigue can weaken restraint. Stress can intensify reactions. Trauma, fear, pressure, and exhaustion can profoundly affect how people respond, and Christians should be careful not to reduce every emotional struggle to a simplistic formula.
But Jesus still teaches us to examine what comes from within.
Pressure can reveal things.
Squeeze a sponge and whatever has soaked into it comes out.
Shake a bottle hard enough and eventually its contents become obvious.
And sometimes life shakes us.
A betrayal shakes us.
A disrespectful child shakes us.
A difficult marriage shakes us.
A financial crisis shakes us.
A comment on Facebook shakes us.
A person who knows exactly where our wounds are shakes us.
Then something comes spilling out.
And afterward we stare at our own words almost like someone else said them.
“Where did that come from?”
Jesus answers:
Look deeper.
Look at the heart.

That does not mean every accidental phrase perfectly defines your entire character. Scripture does not teach that one foolish sentence proves everything about a person. Peter himself spoke rashly and failed terribly, yet Christ restored him.
The issue is not merely one verbal stumble.
The issue is the treasure being accumulated within.
Read the whole thought in Luke 6:45:

“A good man out of the good treasure of his heart bringeth forth that which is good; and an evil man out of the evil treasure of his heart bringeth forth that which is evil: for of the abundance of the heart his mouth speaketh.”
Notice the word:
treasure.
Something has been stored.
That changes the question.
The question is no longer only:
“What did I say?”
It becomes:
“What have I been storing?”
Resentment can be stored.
Envy can be stored.
Pornographic fantasies can be stored.
Bitterness can be stored.
Fear can be stored.
Self-righteousness can be stored.
Years of rehearsed offenses can be stored.
Secret contempt can be stored.
You can smile at somebody every Sunday while quietly depositing resentment toward them Monday through Saturday.
Deposit.
Deposit.
Deposit.
Then one afternoon the vault opens.
And everybody wonders where those words came from.
They came from somewhere.
This is why Scripture had already warned God's people long before the earthly ministry of Jesus:
מִכָּל־מִשְׁמָר נְצֹר לִבֶּךָ כִּי־מִמֶּנּוּ תּוֹצְאוֹת חַיִּים
mikkol-mishmar netsor libbekha, ki-mimmennu tots'ot chayyim
“Keep thy heart with all diligence; for out of it are the issues of life.” — Proverbs 4:23, KJV
לִבֶּךָ — libbekha means “your heart.”
נְצֹר — netsor carries the command to guard, watch, or keep.
And תּוֹצְאוֹת — tots'ot points toward outgoings or what proceeds from a source.
Guard your heart...
because life flows outward from there.
Do you see the connection?
Proverbs tells us to guard the source.
Jesus tells us that the mouth reveals the overflow.
And this is where Christianity becomes far more radical than behavior modification.
Religion without heart transformation says:
Control your mouth.
Jesus goes deeper:
What is filling your heart?
Religion can teach a bitter person Christian vocabulary.
Jesus can transform the bitter person.
Religion can teach an angry man to smile in church.
Jesus wants the anger surrendered.
Religion can teach an envious woman to type, “Congratulations!”
Jesus wants to free her from the jealousy hurting underneath.
Religion can polish the outside.
Jesus goes after the tomb.
Remember His confrontation with the religious leaders.
These were people who knew how to look holy.
They knew ceremonies.
They knew rules.
They knew public spirituality.
Yet Jesus repeatedly exposed the danger of appearing righteous outwardly while corruption remained inwardly.
That should frighten every Christian who has learned how to sound saved without allowing Christ into the locked rooms of the heart.
Because you can know worship lyrics...
and still destroy someone with gossip.
You can post Bible verses...
and still speak to your spouse with contempt.
You can say “God bless you” publicly...
and curse people privately.
You can defend biblical truth online...
while speaking without biblical love.
You can rebuke darkness in the culture...
while protecting darkness inside yourself.
And perhaps the most terrifying version of Christianity is not openly rejecting Jesus.
Perhaps it is learning how to speak Christian while refusing to let Christ search the heart.
David understood the danger.
After grievous sin, he did not merely pray:
“God, help me improve my public image.”
He cried:
“Create in me a clean heart, O God; and renew a right spirit within me.” — Psalm 51:10, KJV
Create.
Not decorate.
Not disguise.
Not manage.
Create.
David understood something many of us spend years avoiding:
Sometimes the problem is not merely what we did.
Something inside us needs the mercy of God.
And this is where the Gospel becomes breathtaking.
Because if Jesus only exposed hearts, none of us could stand comfortably before Him.
Think about everything He knows.
Every jealous thought.
Every lustful imagination.
Every whispered insult.
Every prayer spoken publicly while pride secretly wanted admiration.
Every cruel sentence you rehearsed but were wise enough not to say.
Every hidden motive.
Every grudge.
Every moment you wanted revenge.
Every time your mouth worshiped while your heart wandered.
He knows.
And still...
the cross happened.
That is the scandal of grace.
The One who knows the darkest rooms of the human heart walked willingly toward Calvary for sinners.
Jesus did not die because humanity needed better vocabulary.
He died because humanity needed redemption.
Our deepest problem cannot be solved by merely learning to speak more politely.
We need forgiveness.
We need reconciliation with God.
We need cleansing.
We need new life.
We need Christ.
At the cross, Jesus carried sin and bore judgment so that those who repent and trust in Him may be forgiven and reconciled to God.
And here is what makes grace so astonishing:
Jesus does not merely forgive the words that came out.
He begins transforming the heart they came from.
That is the difference between shame and conviction.
Shame whispers:
“Hide.”
The Gospel says:
“Come into the light.”
Shame says:
“If people knew what was inside you, they would abandon you.”
Jesus says:
“I already know. Repent and come to Me.”
Grace does not call evil good.
Grace tells the truth about evil and then points sinners toward the Savior.
Maybe that is why you needed this article today.
Maybe there is a sentence you cannot forget.
Something you said to your wife.
Something you screamed at your husband.
Something your child still remembers.
Something you wrote online.
Something you said about somebody who trusted you.
You apologized.
But perhaps God wants to do more than repair the sentence.
Perhaps He is putting His finger on the wound beneath it.
Maybe beneath the anger is fear.
Beneath the sarcasm is insecurity.
Beneath the gossip is envy.
Beneath the criticism is pride.
Beneath the constant defensiveness is an identity that has forgotten how secure it can be in Christ.
Beneath the harshness is pain you never surrendered.
And Jesus is not exposing it because He delights in humiliating you.
He exposes darkness to bring us into truth.
A surgeon reveals the wound because healing requires reaching what is underneath.
So ask Him.
Not casually.
Not religiously.
Ask Him with terrifying sincerity:
“Jesus, what has my mouth been revealing about my heart?”
Then become quiet enough to listen.
Think about the patterns.
Who brings out the cruelest version of you?
What subject immediately makes you defensive?
Whose success makes you uncomfortable?
Whose failure secretly satisfies you?
What do you repeatedly complain about?
What do you say when you believe nobody important is listening?
How do you speak about people who cannot benefit you?
How do you speak when you are angry?
How do you speak to people with less power than you?
How do you speak about your enemies?
Your words may be leaving fingerprints.
Follow them back to the heart.
But do not stop there.
Because Christianity is not endless self-inspection.
Christianity is Christ.
Bring what you discover to Him.
Confess it.
Repent.
Receive His mercy.
Ask the Holy Spirit to cultivate what human effort cannot manufacture permanently.
Jesus said the good person brings good from the good treasure of the heart.
So begin asking another question:
“What am I storing?”
If your heart is continually fed outrage, do not be surprised when outrage becomes your language.
If your mind continually consumes lust, do not be surprised when people slowly become objects in your imagination.
If you spend hours feeding comparison, do not be surprised when gratitude becomes difficult.
But fill yourself with the Word of God.
Remember the Gospel.
Meditate on Christ.
Practice gratitude.
Forgive because you have been forgiven.
Pray for the people you are tempted to hate.
Remember how patiently Jesus has dealt with you.
Then something begins changing.
Not instantly perfect.
Not fake.
Not performative.
But transformed over time.
The mouth begins learning the language of a heart increasingly surrendered to Christ.
Where there was gossip, restraint begins growing.
Where there was cruelty, gentleness appears.
Where there was constant complaining, gratitude begins breathing.
Where there was condemnation, truth begins walking beside mercy.
Where there was pride, humility starts saying:
“I was wrong.”
Where there was hatred, grace learns to pray:
“Lord, have mercy on them...and have mercy on me.”
That is transformation.
And sometimes one of the clearest evidences of spiritual maturity is not how loudly somebody worships when the music is playing.
It is how they speak when they are wounded.
Jesus Himself said:
“For out of the abundance of the heart his mouth speaketh.”
So perhaps today is not primarily about cleaning up your vocabulary.
Perhaps it is about surrendering your reservoir.
Let Christ deal with what has been accumulating there.
The resentment.
The jealousy.
The wounds.
The pride.
The lust.
The anger.
The secret hatred.
The exhausting need to prove yourself.
Bring it into the light.
There is grace for repentant sinners.
There is forgiveness in Christ.
There is restoration.
There is a new beginning.
And perhaps somebody reading this has spent years believing that because ugly things came from their heart, they are beyond redemption.
Look at Peter.
He denied Jesus.
Not silently.
With his mouth.
The same Peter who declared loyalty collapsed under pressure and denied knowing the Lord.
Imagine remembering those words.
Imagine hearing yourself deny the One you loved.
Yet failure was not the final chapter of Peter's story.
The risen Christ restored him.
Grace rewrote what shame wanted to make permanent.
That does not make sin insignificant.
It makes Jesus magnificent.
This is the heartbeat behind Gospel Warrior:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Not by calling sin harmless.
Not by covering darkness with inspirational language.
Jesus enters the wreckage with truth and grace, calls sinners to repentance, forgives those who come to Him in faith, and begins making people new.
Think about the last thing you said that you deeply regret.
Don't excuse it yet.
Follow it backward.
What was underneath it?
Ask Jesus to show you.
And if this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not have to tell strangers every detail. But you can stop pretending.
Somebody else may need evidence tonight that sanctification is real and God is not finished with them.
Not because every word here is important.
Because the words of Jesus are.
Come back to Luke 6:45 the next time anger rises and your mouth is preparing to release what your heart has been storing.
Not to build an algorithm.
Not to make a page famous.
The glory belongs to Christ alone.
do not leave without hearing what Jesus is saying.
Your mouth matters.
But your heart matters more.
The answer is not learning to hide the overflow better.
The answer is bringing the source to Christ.
Because someday, by the grace of God, the words that once exposed your bitterness may begin revealing forgiveness.
The mouth that once tore people down may begin building them up.
The tongue that once spread gossip may begin telling people about Jesus.
The voice that once screamed from woundedness may begin praying from healing.
And the person who once whispered, “I can never change,” may someday look backward and realize:
Jesus had been rewriting the story all along.
Your mouth may reveal what has been hiding in your heart—but the heart you surrender to Jesus does not have to remain the heart you brought Him.
